en: 1. This sequence of phonemes originated from Nārāyaṇa:
a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au am aḥ; ka kha ga gha ṅa; ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; ta tha da dha na; pa pha ba bha ma; ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣa.

These are the "vowels" (varṇas), the "syllables" (akṣaras), and the "consonants" (alas). Their places of origin are as follows: the throat is the place of origin for the *ka*-group, *ha*, and *visarga*; the palate is the place of origin for *i*, *ī*, the *ca*-group, and *ya* and *śa*.
The lips are the place of articulation for the *u*-varga, the labials;
the head is the place for the *ṛ*-varga, the cerebrals, and the retroflexes (*ra* and *ṣa*);
the teeth are the place for the *ḷ*-varga, the dentals, and the liquids (*la*).
The *e* and *ai* vowels are produced at the throat and palate;
the *o* and *au* vowels at the throat and lips;
and the letter *va* at the teeth and lips.
"The head of the *anusvāra* is the nose," and so forth. ||1||
2. First, there are fourteen Sarveśvaras.

In that sequence of letters, the first fourteen letters are named Sarveśvara: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au. These are the "vowels" (*svara*) or "vocalic sounds" (*ac*) according to the ancients. They are pronounced independently; since the pronunciation of the consonants beginning with *ka* depends upon them, they are called Sarveśvaras. This should be understood similarly in other contexts as well.
Others maintain that the mere brevity of their duration is like a festival for a son.
By obtaining even a single syllable of the Name of Hari, we disregard such [worldly] things as you. ||2||
3. Ten vowel-stages (*daśāvatāra*).
Among them, first there are ten vowels which are the names of the ten stages: *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, e, ai, o*.
These are the "homogeneous" (*samāna*) vowels, and according to the ancients, they are also called "vowels" (*akaḥ*). ||3||

4. Among those, two by two are of one essence. Among those ten vowels (*daśāvatāra*), it should be understood that two letters at a time, in their respective order, along with the *prapañca*, are each of one essence—just as *a* and *ā* are two of one essence, and *i* and *ī* are two of one essence, and likewise *u* and *ū*, etc. Furthermore, they bear the designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*). Since the fact that each pair is of one essence is already evident, this sūtra is intended for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). ||4||

5. The preceding [vowel] is short (vāmana). Among those [vowels] which consist of a single element, each preceding phoneme is designated by the name "short" (vāmana): a, i, u, ṛ, and ḷ. These are short, as well as the prolated (nirhrasva) vowels. ||5||
6. *Parastrivikrama*. Among those [vowels] consisting of a single essence, the letter that follows the others is named *trivikrama*: *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *è*, *ÿ*. These are the long vowels. ||6||

7. The Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) consists of three morae (*trimātra*). A phoneme (*varṇa*) being uttered with a duration of three morae shall be designated as the "Dwarf" (*vāmana*) and "Three-Strider" (*trivikrama*), and is known as the Great Person. This is well-known in cases such as calling from a distance, singing, and weeping. It is also designated as *pluta* (protracted), as it has been said: "A short vowel (*hrasva*) shall consist of one mora; a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is said to consist of two morae."
The protracted vowel (pluta) should be known as having three moras (mātrās), and a consonant has half a mora.
(A statement from the science of *saura*):

Regarding the three initial [vowels], their conventional usage follows the sequence of the cock’s crow. In this regard, experts pronounce and write even the word "Vāmana" as "Trivikrama" when referring to the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*). "Come, O Viṣṇumitra! Come! "I have come, O Protector of the World! I have come. (7)
8. "'Varjitaḥ sarveśvarā īśvarāḥ'—those devoid of two letters are the 'sarveśvaras,' meaning those named Īśvara: i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, e, ai, o, au. These are the 'nāmins' and the 'icas. (8)
9. The lords are the ten incarnations. "The ten incarnations, excluding [the others], are named Īśa: i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, e, ai, o, au, am. These are the *ika*s. (9)
10. The vowels i, ī, u, ū are infinite; and [the vowel] aṇ [is also infinite]. ||10||
11. *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū* are the four short vowels (*sanāḥ*). And [the vowel] *iṇ* [is also included]. ||11||
12. *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ* are four-syllabled. And [the rule] "of *u*" applies. ||12||

13. *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* are the fourfold manifestations (*caturvyūha*). They are called "diphthongs" (*sandhyakṣara*) and "the *ec*-vowels. All of these indeed possess three steps (*trivikrama*). ||13||

14. *Am* is the discus of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇucakra*). The letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation. The phoneme whose nature is the *bindu* (dot) is named the discus of Viṣṇu; it is also called *anusvāra*, *bindu*, and *lava*. ||14||
15. *Aṃ* is the bow of Viṣṇu.

This phoneme, which has the shape of a half-moon, is named the bow of Viṣṇu and is also called "nasalized" (*anunāsika*). It is so called because it originates from the nose; however, that which is accompanied by nasality (*sānunāsika*) originates from both the mouth and the nose. ||15||
16. *Aḥ* is the emission of Viṣṇu. The phoneme having the form of two dots is named the emission of Viṣṇu; it is also called *visarga*, *visarjanīya*, *visṛṣṭa*, and *abhiniṣṭāna*. ||16||

17. *Kādayo viṇujanāḥ*. The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha* are the names of the progeny of Viṣṇu. Because Viṣṇu is all-pervading, they are dependent upon Him like His subjects; this is the meaning. *Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*; *ca, cha, ja, jha, ña*; *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa*; *ta, tha, da, dha, na*; *pa, pha, ba, bha, ma*; *ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha*. In the combination of *ka* and *ṣa*, however, there is *kṣa*. These are the "consonants" (*vyañjanāni*) and the "hal-sounds" (*halaḥ*). ||17||
18. But the *bala* [syllables] are those excluding *ya* and *va*. And [the *bala* syllables are] *ra*, *la*, and *ṣa*. ||18||

19. Those ending in *m* are five groups of Viṣṇu. Those phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* constitute five groups of Viṣṇu. These are the "groups" (*vargas*). *Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa* is the *kavarga*. Likewise are the *cavarga*, *ṭavarga*, *tavarga*, and *pavarga*.
These are also known by the names *ku*, *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, and *pu*. However, all of them are indeed "contact consonants" (*sparśas*). 19.

20. But the attendants of Viṣṇu are excluded, as is "mayaḥ. In that regard, those belonging to the same class are called "savargaḥ" (of the same class) and "savarṇaḥ" (of the same phonetic quality). ||20||
21. *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* are the [first letters of the classes] corresponding to Hari and Kamalā;
likewise, the first letters and *ca* and *pa*. ||21||
22. Kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ha, ri, kha, ḍa, and gha;
[these are] the "second letters," as well as "cha" and "pha. ||22||
23. *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, *ba* are the *hari-gadas*; [the vowels] *ṛ*, *u*, *i*, *a*, *e*, *o*, *ai*, *au* are the *jabas*. ||23||
24. *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *bha* are the *harighoṣas*; [the term] "fourth letters" refers to *ja*, *bha*, and so forth. ||24||
25. Ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, and mā are the *hariveṇu* sounds; they are the "fifth [consonants]," the "nasals," and the "ñama" group. ||25||

26. Those who are excluded from these are the Viṣṇudāsas. Excluding *hari* and *veṇu*, the Viṣṇu-group consists of those named Viṣṇudāsa. *ka kha ga gha*, *ca cha ja jha*, *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha*, *ta tha da dha*, *pa pha ba bha*—these are the "jhapas. ||26||
27. *Ya-ra-la-vā* are the friends of *ha-ri-mi-trāṇi*;
so too are the *antaḥsthāḥ* (semivowels) and *ṣa-naḥ*. These [groups] are both with the bow of Viṣṇu (*saviṣṇucāpāḥ*) and without the bow of Viṣṇu (*nirviṣṇucāpāḥ*). ||27||
28. Śa, ṣa, sa, and ha belong to the Harigotra;
they are [also known as] "ūṣmāṇaḥ," "ṣitaḥ," and "śalaḥ. ||28||
29. *Śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* are *śauri*. And "*śara*" [is also *śauri*]. ||29||

30. Viṣṇu, Dāsa, and Harigotra are Vaiṣṇavas. These are the names of the Vaiṣṇavas: ka, kha, ga, gha; ca, cha, ja, jha; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha; ta, tha, da, dha; pa, pha, ba, bha; śa, ṣa, sa, ha. These are the "dhuṭs" and the "jhalas. ||30||
31. Hari, gadā, hari-ghoṣa, hari-veṇu, hari-mitra, and ha—the cowherds.
These are the names of the cowherds: ga, gha, ṅa; ja, jha, ña; ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; da, dha, na; ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, la, va, ha. These are the "sonorants" (ghoṣavantaḥ) and the "ha-sounds" (haśaḥ). ||31||

32. The Yādavas are others; those born of Viṣṇu other than the cowherds, bearing the name Yādava—namely: ka, kha, ca, cha, ṭa, ṭha, ta, tha, pa, pha, śa, ṣa, sa. These are the "unvoiced" (*aghoṣa*) and the "harsh" (*khara*). ||32||
33. But the Sātvatas are those excluding Śauri; that is, the Yādavas, excluding Śauri, are named Sātvatas. And [the term] "khapaḥ. 33.
34. The effort (*prayatna*) of all the lords (*sarveśvara*) is without contact (*asparśī*);
that of the classes of Viṣṇu is with contact (*sparśī*); and that of the friends of Hari is slightly with contact (*īṣatsparśī*).
35. [The rule applies] after a vowel (*rāda*), an anusvāra, and before *ya* and *va*.
Without *ya-ra-am*, furthermore, [the term] *viṣṇupada* and so forth [is used] when there is at least a slight contact [with the preceding vowel].
(36) In some cases, from *upendra* [the term] *viṣṇupada* and so forth [occurs].

The designation *upendra* (Ā.pra. 42) and the designation *viṣṇupada* (Vi.pra. 7) will be explained later. It should be understood that [this applies to] *trivikrama*, *mahāpuruṣa*, and *harigotra*. In that regard, it is shown in sequence by means of examples: *aryamā*, *yaṃyamyate*, *ayyate*, *vāyvagnī*, *nārāyaṇāya*, *niyamaḥ*, and *prayuṅkte*. Here, only the fifth and sixth are actual examples; the others, however, are counter-examples. (34–36)
37. *Rāma* in the case of the essential nature of a phoneme (*varṇa*).

When the mere essential nature of a phoneme is to be expressed, the word *rāma* should be employed, because it denotes the singular apprehension [of that phoneme], as in *arāma*, *irāma*, and so forth. Furthermore, *at* and *it* and so on belong to Pāṇini; *akāra* and so on belong to Kalāpa; and *karāma* and so on are likewise used. However, *kakāra* and so on belong to the Easterners (*prācām*). But for *ra*, it is *repha*. ||34||
38. Regarding the two [terms] beginning with *tat*:

when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is specified, the word *dvaya* should be applied to the two [entities] denoted by that beginning. For example, *advayam* (non-duality) and *idvayam ātmā* (this self). Because this denotes Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, it is considered a name of the Blessed One (*bhagavan*). Indeed, its mantra is called the "Dvaya-mantra" in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Furthermore, the expression "the phoneme *a*" (*avarṇa*) and so forth belongs to the ancients, while "the letter *a*" (*akāra*) and so forth belongs to Pāṇini. ||35||
39. Ādeśa is Viriñci. Just as Brahmā, known as Viriñci, takes one substance and creates another, so too the procedure that proceeds in that manner is called both Ādeśa and Viriñci. ||39||
40. Āgama is Viṣṇu. Just as Viṣṇu himself, having manifested from within, becomes the nourisher, so too that ritual procedure which proceeds is called both Āgama and Viṣṇu. ||40||

41. *Lopa* is *hara*. Just as *hara* (the destroyer) becomes the cause of destruction, so too the rule that operates is called both "*lopa*" and "*hara*. In this context, *hara* is twofold: therein, *hara* is the cause of mere non-appearance; *mahāhara* is the cause of absolute dissolution. Others call it "*luk*. ||41||

42. Sūtras are of six kinds: "A designation (saṃjñā), a technical rule (paribhāṣā), an injunction (vidhi), a restriction (niyama), an extension (atideśa), and a governing heading (adhikāra)—this is the sixfold definition of a sūtra. Thus it is said.

Some read "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) and "qualification" (*adhikāra*); here, "naming" (*nāmakaraṇa*) refers to a designation (*saṃjñā*), such as: "First, there are fourteen Sarveśvaras" (Saṃhitā-prakāśa 2), and so forth. Others will be mentioned later. ||42||

43. An unestablished form (*asiddharūpa*) is not to be abandoned; it should be understood as ending with the *kṛt* suffixes. In this grammar, however, unlike elsewhere, an unestablished form is not discarded in every instance along the way. Each such case should be understood as extending up to the end of the *kṛt* section. The meaning is that this does not apply to compounds (*samāsa*) or secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). The rule regarding the *darśanīya* suffix will follow later. ||43||
Thus ends [the section on] perception and so forth.
This section on *sandhi*, consisting of parts set in bold type,
is the *Sarveśvara-sandhi*;
I joyfully begin this composition of phonemes.
Therefore, let my mind be fixed in concentration upon Your dark lotus feet.

Sandhi is obligatory within a single word and obligatory between a verbal root and a prefix; it is considered non-obligatory in the formulation of grammatical rules and non-obligatory elsewhere as well.

This is a general rule (*paribhāṣā*). And it serves as a regulator where there is no fixed rule. 44. A phoneme (*varṇa*) that applies throughout all sections, which is caused by a mere phoneme, may be a modification (*vikāra*) or a euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), depending on the specific context in some cases.
Furthermore:
45. All those *ya* sounds that are joined to a consonant (*hal*) following a vowel (*ac*) are considered to be [part of the preceding vowel];
and that [consonant] is also [considered part of the vowel] where it does not end in *ra*, *ma*, or another vowel, nor is it separated by a foot-break (*aṅghribheda*).

And then, with "kṛṣṇa" standing before "agre," according to the maxim that "for the sake of the intended meaning, one may separate or join a syllable," there is the separation of the vowel 'a' (arāma), resulting in "kṛṣṇ + a + agre. And then... ||44||

46. When the ten incarnations (*daśāvatāra*) merge into the single essence (*ekātman*), they become Trivikrama. When the phoneme named "ten incarnations" merges with the supreme single-essence phoneme, it becomes Trivikrama. Furthermore, there is the merging of *ārāma* again—namely, before *kṛṣṇa*. Thus: *rādhā* + *āgatā* = *rādhāgatā*; *hari* + *iti* = *harīti*; *hari* + *īhā* = *harīhā*; *viṣṇu* + *udayaḥ* = *viṣṇūdayaḥ*; *viṣṇu* + *ūḍhā* = *viṣṇūḍhā*; *narabhrātṛ* + *ṛṣiḥ* = *bhrātṛṣiḥ*; *gamṛ* + *ṛkāraḥ* = *gamṛṛkāraḥ*. ||46||
47. The identity of two *ṛ* sounds with one another must be stated;
likewise for two *ṛ* sounds, two *ṝ* sounds, two *ḷ* sounds, two *ḹ* sounds, and so forth. Such a rule is *viriñci*: a *vidhi* is an instruction regarding what ought to be done. ||47||

48. When *i* or *ī* follows a non-dual (*advaya*) vowel, it becomes *e*. Thus, when these two vowels follow a non-dual vowel, they merge to form *erāma*. For example: *yādava* + *indraḥ* = *yādavendraḥ*; *gokula* + *īśaḥ* = *gokuleśaḥ*; *mathurā* + *īśaḥ* = *mathureśaḥ*. ||41||

49. Or likewise in the case of *pra* followed by *eṣa* and *eṣya*. When *pra* precedes *eṣa* and *eṣya*, a sandhi may optionally occur in the same manner. *pra* + *eṣaḥ* = *preṣaḥ*; *pra* + *eṣyaḥ* = *preṣyaḥ*. In the alternative case, when there is a pair of *e*s, they become *ai*: *praiṣaḥ*, *praiṣyaḥ*. ||49||

50. When two vowels [occur], namely *a* and *ā*, or when two [vowels] *u* and *ū* follow, they merge to become *o* and *au*. Here, the term "not two" (*advayam*) from the preceding rule is understood to carry over. As it has been said:
"A grammatical element is superseded by another grammatical element; a grammatical operation is superseded by another grammatical operation."
"And that which remains follows by means of the [preceding] sign and the sign itself.
Thus: *puruṣa* + *uttamaḥ* = *puruṣottamaḥ*, *suparṇa* + *ūḍhaḥ* = *suparṇoḍhaḥ*, *dvārakā* + *utsavaḥ* = *dvārakotsavaḥ*. ||50||
51. And likewise for *omi*:
*kṛṣṇa* + *oṃ* = *kṛṣṇom*. ||51||

52. When the two vowels *a* and *ā* are followed by the pair *ṛ* and *ṝ*, or when the two vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* are followed by the pair *e* and *ai*, they merge to become *ar*. For example: *kṛṣṇa* + *ṛddhiḥ* = *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*. ||52||

53. In the case of two [consonants], *a*, *l*, and *ā* constitute one pair; when followed by the two [consonants] *ṣ* and *ṣṣ*, they merge to become *al*. Thus, *yamunā* + *ṣkārāyate* = *yamunalkārāyate*. ||53||
54. Furthermore, in the *Advayasandhi* [section], the substitution of *ā* should be stated as if it were the subsequent cause (*paranimittavat*).

This is an extension (*atideśa*)—an extension is the prescription of similarity to something else. Here, it will be stated that the *ṅit*-status of *āṅ* applies when it is joined with a verb (Saṃkṣiptasāraprakriyā 70). *ā* + *ihi* = *ehi*; *kṛṣṇa* + *ihi* = *kṛṣṇehi*. *ā* + *ūḍhā* = *oḍhā*; *kṛṣṇa* + *ūḍhā* = *kṛṣṇoḍhā*. *ā* + *ṛddhiḥ* = *ṛddhiḥ*; *kṛṣṇa* + *ṛddhiḥ* = *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*. *ā* + *ṿkārāyate* = *ṿkārāyate*; *yamunā* + *ṿkārāyate* = *yamunalkārāyate*. ॥54॥

55. Regarding *edvaye ai*: when the two vowels *e* and *o* are followed by another pair [of vowels], they merge to become *air*. For example: *kṛṣṇa* + *ekanāthaḥ* = *kṛṣṇaikanāthaḥ*; *kṛṣṇa* + *aiśvaryam* = *kṛṣṇaiśvaryam*.
56. *svādīreriṇośca tathā*: likewise, after a long vowel (*sū*), *ā*, *ī*, or *ṛ*, [the same rule applies].
*sva* + *īram* = *svairam*; *sva* + *īrī* = *svairī* and *svairiṇī*. This is because of the maxim that when a word is mentioned, it includes its forms distinguished by gender as well. ||56||

57. Regarding the rule "odvaye au": when the two vowels *o* and *au* are followed by two vowels combined, they become *aurāma*. For example: *kṛṣṇa* + *odanaṃ* = *kṛṣṇaudanam*; *kṛṣṇa* + *aunnatyaṃ* = *kṛṣṇaunnatyam*. ||57||
58. And likewise in the case of *pra* before *ūḍha* and *ūḍhi*.

*pra* + *ūḍhaḥ* = *prauḍhaḥ*; *pra* + *ūḍhiḥ* = *prauḍhiḥ*. Some read it as *ūha*, [resulting in] *prauhaḥ*. But here [the form] *prauḍhavān* does not occur, according to the principle that when a meaningful element is mentioned, that which is meaningless is not included. ||58||

59. Regarding the two vowels *i* and *ī*: when the two vowels *i* and *ī* occur before the Supreme Lord (the letter *r*), they remain as two distinct sounds and do not merge. In the case of *ya*, the suffix *arāma* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The same applies elsewhere as well. Examples: *hari* + *arcanaṃ* = *haryarcanam* *hari* + *āsanaṃ* = *haryāsanam* *dadhi* + *upendrasya* = *dadhyupendrasya* *rukmiṇī* + *eṣā* = *rukmiṇyeṣā*

In the section on duality, the proof is established by this much alone. However, other great alternatives will be stated later. Therefore, the proposition that "that which is unestablished in form must not be abandoned" (Saṃvitprakāśa 43) does not fail here.

How is it "hari-hari"? It is by relying on their identity as one essence (*ekātmakatā*), because the rule for the specific case (*viśeṣa*) of Trivikrama is more powerful. For instance: that which pervades the whole is the universal (*sāmānya*); that which pervades only a part is the particular (*viśeṣa*). The universal rule is the general (*utsarga*); the particular rule is the exception (*apavāda*). This being established: between the preceding and the following, the following rule is stronger; between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the non-obligatory (*anitya*), the obligatory prevails; between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*), the internal prevails; and between the general and the exceptional, the exceptional prevails. And among these, each subsequent [rule] is stronger than the preceding.

If there were a state of commonality among the ten incarnations (*daśāvatāra*), then the term "non-duality" (*advaya*) alone would have been used; for even in cases such as "two Viṣṇus," the application of the subsequent rule [of *dvandva*] would necessarily follow. Thus, these and other logical principles, being accepted through both reasoning and established tradition, pervade both the preceding and the succeeding portions of the text. (59)
60. *udvayaṃ vaḥ*. When the two sounds *u* and *ū* occur before the supreme *eśvara*, they become *o*. For example: *madhu* + *ariḥ* = *madhvariḥ*; *viṣṇu* + *āśritaḥ* = *viṣṇvāśritaḥ*. ||60||

61. *Ṛ* and *Ṝ*: When *ṛ* and *è* are followed by *sarveśvara*, they become *ra* and *rāma* respectively. *rāmabhrātṛ* + *udayaḥ* = *rāmabhrātrudayaḥ*; *rāmabhrātṛ* + *aiśvaryam* = *rāmabhrātraiśvaryam*. ||61||

62. *ÿ* and *dvayaṃ laḥ*. The two sounds *ÿ* and *ÿ* (representing *ṣ* and *ś*) become *la* (the letter *l*) when followed by *sarveśvara* (the letter *r*). For example, *śakÿ* + *arthaḥ* = *śaklarthaḥ*; this is according to Śrīpati alone. According to the opinion of Vyāḍi and Gālava, the letters *ya*, *va*, *ra*, and *la* occur only in the middle [of a word]: for instance, *hariyarcanaṃ*, *madhuvariḥ*, *bhuvādi*, and so forth. //50//
63. And this [is] the meaning: excellence in Kṛṣṇa, who is the supreme Lord of all—this is "excellence in Kṛṣṇa" (kṛṣṇotkarṣaḥ). ||63||

64. *ai* becomes *āy* when followed by *airāmaḥ* (the group of vowels beginning with *ai*), provided that *sarveśvara* follows: *yamunāyai* + *arghaḥ* = *yamunāyāyarghaḥ*; *gopyai* + *āsanam* = *gopyāyāsanam*. ||64||
65. When *o* or *ava* becomes *av*, and when followed by *sarveśvara*, *para*, or *viṣṇu*: *iha* = *iha*. Thus, *viṣṇu + iha* becomes *viṣṇaviha*.
66. *au* becomes *āv* when followed by *sarveśvara*—for example, *kṛṣṇau* + *atra* = *kṛṣṇāvatra*.
67. Elision of *e* and *o* before *a* at the end of a *viṣṇupada*.
When *e* and *o* are situated at the end of a *viṣṇupada*, there is elision of a following *a* or *ā*. *hare* + *atra* = *hare'tra*; *viṣṇo* + *atra* = *viṣṇo'tra*. ||67||

68. *Ayādīnāṃ yavayor vā*. For these [words] beginning with *aya*—namely *aya*, *āya*, and *āva*—there is the elision (*hara*) of either *ya* or *va* when followed by the feet of Viṣṇu (the vowels), provided they are within the scope of the rule. Examples: *kṛṣṇayutkarṣaḥ* = *kṛṣṇa utkarṣaḥ*; *yamunāyāyarghaḥ* = *yamunāyā arghaḥ*; *gopyāyāsanam* = *gopyā āsanam*; *viṣṇaviha* = *viṣṇa iha*; *kṛṣṇāvatra* = *kṛṣṇā atra*. These two [consonants], *ya* and *va*, are considered to be slightly touching (*īṣatsparśinau*) and slightly touching sounds (*īṣatsparśitarau*). 68.

69. For those [words] ending in *y* or *v*, the sandhi is not obligatory. For those words ending in *y* or *v*, sandhi does not necessarily occur; this is a prohibition. Examples include: *kṛṣṇa utkarṣaḥ*, *yamunāyarghaÿh*, *gopyāsanam*, *viṣṇa iha*, and so forth. 69.

70. Regarding the indeclinables ending in *o* and *ām*, when followed by the word *sarveśvara*: when the indeclinables ending in *o* and *ām*, whether finite or not, and those that are purely indeclinables, are followed by the word *sarveśvara*, there is no euphonic combination (*sandhi*) between the preceding and the following words—e.g., *no upendraḥ*, *no acyutaḥ*. How is it that in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), when the word *go-* ending in the suffix *-vipra-* is an indeclinable, we have *go'bhavat*? In the case of *go'bhavat*, the rule applies because of the maxim: "between a term defined by a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*) and one stated directly in a rule (*pratipadokta*), the directly stated one alone is to be taken. Thus it would be so.

The particles *ara*, *ā*, and others are used in address (*sambodhana*) and other senses. Among these: in address—*a ananta!*; in recollection—*ā evam acyuta-līlā!*; in reproach—*i acyutaṃ na bhajasi*; in filling out a sentence (*vāk-pūraṇa*)—*ī īdṛśaḥ saṃsāraḥ*; in calling out (*āmantraṇa*)—*u acyuta!*; in prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)—*u upasannaṃ māṃ tyajasi*. However, a sandhi does indeed occur with *āṅ*: *ā anantam* = *ānantam*, meaning "having set a limit that is infinite. Regarding this, it is said: "One should know that *ā* is marked with *ṅ* (āṅ) when it signifies slightness, connection with an action, pervasion, or a limit; but it is unmarked (*aṅ*) in sentences and in recollection. (70)
71. *Īt*, *ūt*, and *et* [ending] in the dual number do not undergo euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) when followed by *sarveśvara*, except in the case of *maṇīva* and others.

Regarding those forms ending in *ī*, *ū*, *e*, *ām*, and *āṇ* that stand in the place of the dual number, no *saṃdhi* occurs when *sarveśvara* follows. Examples: *harī atra*, *viṣṇū atra*, *amū atra*, *gaṅge atra*, *bhajete ajitam*, *amūke atra staḥ*. However, the followers of Candra desire *saṃdhi* here: *amūke'tra staḥ*. But in the case of *maṇīva* and others, *saṃdhi* certainly does occur; according to some, there is an option (*vikalpa*). For example: *maṇī iva* = *maṇīva*; likewise, *dampatī + iva* = *dampatīva*; *rodasī + iva* = *rodasīva*.
jampatī + iva = jampatīva ||71||

72. Regarding the rule *adaso'mī*: there is no euphonic combination (*sandhi*) for the word *amī* when it is connected with the word *adas*, provided that *sarveśvara* follows it—as in *amī acyutapriyāḥ*. Why "amī"? [Consider: *amūke'tra syuḥ*. According to the followers of Pāṇini, vowels ending in *r* or *ā*, and those beginning with *ā*, are designated as *pragṛhya*.
73. And in the case of *mahāpuruṣa*. In connection with the word *mahāpuruṣa*, when it refers to the Supreme Lord (*pare*), no euphonic combination (*sandhi*) takes place. ||73||

74. The status of being a *mahāpuruṣa* (great person) is recognized in the case of the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*) when there is a distant call and so forth. For example: "Come, O Hari! Come! "Stay, O Hari! Stay here! In the case of the Supreme Lord of All, there is no elision (*niṣedha*) [of the final vowel], but here there is a *sandhi* (euphonic combination). "Go, O Ācyutadatta! Go, O Ācyutadatta! This is an address to the Primordial Great Person (*ādimahāpuruṣa*). For it is said in the relevant sūtras: "In cases such as a distant call, or when there is a special effort, the *saṃsāra* (elision) of the word of address at the end of a sentence does not occur; this is the *mahāpuruṣa*. A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words delimited by an action (*kriyā*). //74//

75. The final vowels, as well as those beginning with *sarveśvara*, are designated as *saṃsāra*; they also bear the designation *ṭi*. Examples include: *āgaccha hare3* (Come, O Hari! and *tiṣṭha hare3* (Stay, O Hari!). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the *Sārasvata* and other grammars include singing, weeping, and deliberation; while the *Kāśikā* states it applies to mere address (*sambodhana*). For instance: *kṛṣṇaṃ bhajasva vaiṣṇavā3!* (Worship Kṛṣṇa, O Vaiṣṇava!). This occurs only at the end of a sentence, but not here—as in *hare āgaccha* (O Hari, come) or *kṛṣṇā3 ehi* (O Kṛṣṇa, come)—which is an error in the *Prakriyākaumudī* (Pāṇini 6.1.125). There are many errors present in the *Sārasvataprakriyā*.
They cannot be fully written down, but they should be understood by following this [text].
That which is unknown to all is recognized as an error;
that which is unknown to many is held to be the opinion of some. (75)
76. But when *hai* and *he* are employed, [the prolated vowel occurs] even after those two final syllables:
*hai3 kṛṣṇa!*; *he3 kṛṣṇa!*; *kṛṣṇa hai3!*; *kṛṣṇa he3!* ||76||
77. In the formula of the return-greeting, there is the word *saṃsāra* (or *saṃvatsara*), but not in the case of women or Śūdras.
After one has said, "I greet you, Viṣṇumitra," the teacher replies: "May you be long-lived, O Viṣṇumitra! (with the protracted vowel).

He states the specific application for the previously mentioned rules: 78. According to the opinion of the ancient teachers (*prācām*), in the case of addressing each individual syllable that is long (*guru*) or even long by position (*ananta*), provided it is not preceded by *ṛ* or *ām*, the vocative particle *mahāpuruṣaḥ* should be used; however, this does not apply according to the views of others. 78.
79. Vāmana is light (laghu). 80. Trivikrama is heavy (guru).
81. Due to association with the virtuous, even Vāmana becomes heavy.

82. A group of Viṣṇu-devotees joined together is designated as *satsaṅga* (association with the good), and this is also called *saṃyoga*. [Examples: *viṣṇumitra-viṣṇūtṛtīyitra*; according to another opinion, simply *viṣṇumitrā3*. Why [is it] not so in the case of *anṛta*? [Example: *kṛṣṇamī3tra*, *kṛṣṇamitrā3*. The word *āgaccha* (come) should be applied at the beginning of every [example], because of the governing rule concerning sentences (*vākya*). ||82||
83. In response to a question, the particle *haivā* may be used. For example: "Did you make a garland, Viṣṇumitra? "Indeed I did (*akārṣaṃ hī3*)," or "Indeed I did (*akārṣaṃ hi*). 83.

84. In a statement containing a reductio ad absurdum (*ākṣepagarbha*), or in a restatement of an opponent's position that has been refuted, there may be a repetition of the sentence. For example: "Do you say that devotion to Hari is impermanent? [The opponent says: "But it is not so in my view. //84//
85. When used for reproaching or in a sense of succession, a reduplicated word takes the *āmreḍita* designation.
For example: "O non-Vaiṣṇava! Non-Vaiṣṇava! Non-Vaiṣṇava! Non-Vaiṣṇava! (avaiṣṇavā3, avaiṣṇava, avaiṣṇava, avaiṣṇavā3).

86. When the verb *aṅga* is joined with [another] verb, there is a connection (*saṃsāra*) [between them], and there is expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatā*) in the sense of reproach (*bhartsane*). For example: "O, Hari! Be satisfied [with me]—otherwise, you will now experience suffering. Here, the word "now" (*idānīm*) and so forth constitute the expectancy. Without this, however, such a connection would not occur. 87. In the case of deliberation (*vicāre*), there is a connection with the preceding sentence.
Is it a *tamāla* tree, or is it Krishna? ||87||
88. And *pratiśravaṇa* (response) pertains to *saṃsāra*.

*Pratiśravaṇa* means acceptance, a formal promise (*pratijñāna*), and being oriented toward hearing. [Examples: "Give me the mantra of Hari. "I give the mantra of Hari. "Devotion to Hari ought to be constant. "O Viṣṇumitra! What do you say? Other cases should be understood in the same way. Regarding deliberation, questioning, and worship, the fourfold arrangement (*caturvyūha*) will be explained.
89. There is indeed haste for the first half, for [the vowels] i and u belong to the latter;
therefore, from that which has its parts divided, śara becomes doubled.
"O Hara, is this your umbrella? "No, it is a cloth," he replied. ||89||

90. For *orāma*, which has the Buddha as its cause (*buddhanimitta*), there is optionally this euphonic combination (*sandhi*) when followed by the word *iti*. That is to say, for that *orāma* which has the Buddha as its cause, there may be a *sandhi* when the word *iti* follows. The designation "Buddha" will be explained [in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, 24]. Thus: *viṣṇo iti* or *viṣṇaviti*. Why "which has the Buddha as its cause"? Consider the example: *gavityayamāha* ("He said 'go'"). Here, because the distinction between the original form (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, and because it lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), the designation "Buddha" does not apply; consequently, the euphonic combination prescribed for *viṣṇubhakti* (Viṣṇupurāṇa, 1) is not applicable. The designation "Buddha" will also be explained [there]. 90.
91. Regarding the term *īśa* when it has multiple meanings:

for the one designated as *īśa*, when it refers to the Supreme Lord (*pare*) who is the sole self among all other lords, there may optionally be a *sandhi* (euphonic combination), such as *trivikramasya vāmanaśca* or *hari āsanam*. Or [in other cases], as in *rukmiṇi eṣā* or *rukmiṇī eṣā*, the option is not desired because it is considered non-eternal; the meaning is that there would be no *sandhi* when there is a deliberate pause in pronunciation in the middle. In the case of the *sūtras* designated as *saṃhitā*, however, the option is allowed even when the pronunciation is rapid. 91.
92. Regarding *ṛ* followed by *ṛ* or *dvi-ṛ*:

when *ṛ* follows these two, the sandhi may optionally occur; for example, *trivikramasya vāmanaśca vā* [may become] *sraṣṭṛṛṣabhaḥ* or *yādavaṛṣabhaḥ*. As in Māgha’s verse (6.61): *himaṛtāvapi tāḥ sma bhṛśasvidaḥ*. Also, *mālāṛṣabhasya* or *mālaṛṣabhasya*. In the alternative case, it remains as prescribed, such as *haryāsanam*, etc.

93. The prohibitions regarding the *vāmana* (shortening) do not apply in a *nitya*-compound, nor when it occurs at the end of a *viṣṇupada* (a compound ending in *īśvara*, etc.). [Examples: *haryarthaṃ*, *kumāryau*.

94. There is the absence of *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) after *u* and *ū*; [the substitutes] *ūṃ*, *vaḥ*, and *cet* [are used] for *iti*. 95. After the group beginning with *viṣṇu*, *vaḥ* is optionally used for *iti* before *sarveśvara*. [The forms] *u* and *ū* are used for *iti*. Examples: *kimu uktaṃ* becomes *kimūktam*. One should also understand that *kimu iti* and *kimvitī* are likewise valid. Why "after the group beginning with *viṣṇu*"? [Example: *nañūktam*. [Examples such as] *adyeva*, *halīṣā*, *prārcchati*, *ṛṇārṇam*, *so'gram*, and *gavendra* will be explained later under the sections on compounds (*samāsa*) and verbal derivatives (*taddhita*), because they are difficult to understand. 94–95. [End of section].
Thus ends the Sandhi of Sarveśvara.

Now, the junction with *viṣṇujan* (96): When *viṣṇu* ends in a foot [of a verse] and *harighoṣa* follows, as well as when *harigadā* follows *viṣṇu* ending in a foot, and even when not ending in a foot, the phoneme named *viṣṇudāsa*—the third letter of its respective class (*varga*)—is substituted according to the principle that "in place [of the original], that which is most similar [should stand]. For example: *vāk + acyutasya* = *vāgacyutasya*; *vāk + govindasya* = *vāggovindasya*; *ṣaṭ + gopikāḥ* = *ṣaḍgopikāḥ*; *bhagavat + icchā* = *bhagavadicchā*; *kakubh + viṣṇoḥ* = *kakubviṣṇoḥ*.
Except after *viṣṇupada*, [the elision of the case-ending] does not occur; for example, *kaṃsajit* + *e* becomes *kaṃsajite*.

97. *Hariveṇau hariveṇur vā*: When *viṣṇudāsa* ending in *viṣṇupada* occurs before *hariveṇu*, it may optionally become *hariveṇu*. That [substitution] is the fifth letter of the class (*nivarga*)—*jagat + nāthaḥ* = *jagannāthaḥ*; *jagadnāthaḥ*. *kṛṣṇaguṇ + juṅure* = *kṛṣṇaguṃjuṅure*.
98. The term *harikamala* applies only when [the word] *yādava* follows.

*Viṣṇudāsa* would be the first example of that class when another *yādava* follows—e.g., *vāk-kṛṣṇasya* (the speech of Kṛṣṇa). In this case, the present rule is intended to prevent the application of *harigada* at the end of the word *viṣṇu*. Because of the inclusion of the word *mātra* ("only"), it also applies when not at the end of the word *viṣṇu*. Examples will follow later. ॥63॥

99. *tataḥ śaścho vā*. After the letter *śa*, the letter *cha* may optionally be substituted for *śa*. Thus, after *viṣṇudāsa*, the word *śarāma* becomes either *charāma* or *śarāma*; *suvākśauriḥ* becomes either *suvākśauriḥ* or *suvākchauriḥ*; and *apśāyī* becomes *apchāyī*.
100. It should not be said that [the suffix] *ś* does not undergo elision (*ścyuti*), for [in the case of the word] *vāk*, the *ś* does indeed elide. ||100||

101. *ho* becomes *harighoṣaḥ*. After *viṣṇudāsa*, *ha* may be elided, or the fourth letter of that group [the sibilant] may be substituted—thus, *vāk + hareḥ* becomes *vāgghareḥ*. *ac + halau* becomes *ajjhalau*, *ajhalau*. *ṣaṭ + hareḥ* becomes *ṣaḍḍhareḥ*, *ṣadareḥ*. *tat + halinaḥ* becomes *taddhalinaḥ*, *tadhalinaḥ*. *kakubh + harasya* becomes *kakubbharasya*, *kakubharasya*. ||101||

102. *d* and *t* are always [retained] before the *c*-group and *ṭ*-group consonants. When *l*, *r*, *m*, or *ś* follows, and when the *c*-group or *ṭ*-group follows, that very following letter shall always remain—as in: *tad lakṣmīpateḥ* = *tallakṣmīpateḥ*; *tat caturbhujasya* = *taccaturbhujasya*. *kaṃsajit chādayati* (by rule 98 of the *Saṃkṣiptasāraprakriyā*, etc., applicable to all Yādavas) = *kaṃsajicchādayati*; *tat janārdanasya* = *tajjanārdanasya*; *kaṃsajit jhaṅkāraḥ* = *kaṃsajijjhaṅkāraḥ* (Viṣṇudāsa, *Saṃkṣiptasāraprakriyā*).

By these and other such rules, there is the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *kaṃsa-jit-ṅkāraḥ*). Thus, one says *taññarāmaḥ* or *taññarāmaḥ*. According to that view, by the principle "that which was previously established is not considered as having been accomplished" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*, Pāṇini 8.2.1), only the third letter of that same varga remains. This applies likewise in the case of *parāma*. For example: *kaṃsajit + ṭīkate* = *kaṃsajiṭṭīkate*; *kaṃsajit + ḍhaukate* = *kaṃsajiḍḍhaukate*. ||66||
